findings.requirement_type: Minimum Limits — General Liability (Sacramento + Maricopa)
findings.contract_quote: Building Trades General Aggregate: $2,000,000; Products Comp/Op Aggregate: $2,000,000; Personal & Adv. Injury: $1,000,000; Each Occurrence: $1,000,000; Fire Damage: $100,000. ... Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance and, if necessary, Commercial Umbrella insurance with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §III.A, Page 2 of 4 / Maricopa §8.2.10, Page 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: No Commercial General Liability policy was provided in the program submission. The only policy supplied was a Management Liability package (D&O / EPLI / Fiduciary / Crime).
findings.policy_page: N/A — no GL policy in program
findings.gap_description: Both counties require a Commercial General Liability policy with specific limits, ISO CG 0001 occurrence form (Sacramento), blanket contractual, no XCU exclusion, no third-party action-over restriction (Maricopa). The only policy in the program submission is a Management Liability policy, which provides ZERO coverage for premises bodily injury, products liability, completed operations, or contractual liability. This is a complete coverage absence relative to what both counties require — not a sublimit issue.
findings.plain_english: Run-Test currently has no general liability insurance in the program we received. Both Sacramento and Maricopa County contracts mandate it. Until we confirm a separate GL policy is in force, Run-Test is in material breach of both county contracts the moment work begins, and any third-party bodily-injury claim — a county worker tripping on a ballot pallet, a poll worker hurt by election equipment — would be paid out of Run-Test's checking account. This is the single largest exposure on the balance sheet.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether a CGL policy exists outside of what was submitted. If it does, audit it immediately — it must be ISO CG 0001 occurrence form, $2M/$4M/$4M to satisfy Maricopa (Sacramento's $1M/$2M is satisfied by Maricopa-spec), with blanket Additional Insured (CG 20 10 + CG 20 37), Primary & Noncontributory (CG 20 01 or equivalent), Blanket Waiver of Subrogation, and no XCU/contractual restrictions. If no GL policy exists, bind one immediately — operating under either contract without GL is a material breach.
discoveryQuestions: Run-Test's two largest county contracts — Sacramento and Maricopa — both require a Commercial General Liability policy. Do you know which carrier is on the GL today, and when did you last see the actual policy versus just the certificate?
If a county employee slipped on a ballot pallet at one of your delivery sites tomorrow, who responds — your insurance, the county's, or your bank account?
Has anyone walked you through what's actually inside your GL versus what these contracts require, line-by-line?
When was the last time your broker compared your GL form to the ISO CG 0001 occurrence form your contracts demand?

findings.requirement_type: Minimum Limits — Commercial Auto (Sacramento + Maricopa)
findings.contract_quote: Commercial Automobile Liability for Corporate/business owned vehicles including non-owned and hired, $1,000,000 Combined Single Limit. ... Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit for bodily injury and property damage of not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence with respect to any of the Contractor's owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §III.B, Page 2 of 4 / Maricopa §8.2.11, Page 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: No Commercial Auto policy was provided in the program submission.
findings.policy_page: N/A — no Commercial Auto policy in program
findings.gap_description: Both contracts require Commercial Auto with owned, hired, and non-owned coverage — Sacramento at $1M CSL, Maricopa at $2M CSL. Run-Test physically transports printed ballots, election mail, and high-value election technology equipment between facilities and county sites. The Management Liability policy in the program does not provide any auto coverage.
findings.plain_english: Run-Test moves ballots and election equipment by truck. There is no commercial auto policy in the program we received. If a Run-Test driver causes an accident transporting ballots, the resulting bodily injury and property damage claim has no insurance behind it — and either county contract is in material breach. Auto judgments routinely exceed $1M; commercial-vehicle accidents involving fatalities can hit $5M-$10M.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Auto policy exists outside this submission. It must support $2M CSL (Maricopa is the controlling threshold) covering owned (Symbol 1), hired (Symbol 8), and non-owned (Symbol 9) vehicles. Add blanket Additional Insured, Primary & Noncontributory, Waiver of Subrogation, MCS-90 if any interstate freight, and the broad Drive-Other-Car / Employee Hired Auto endorsements. If no auto policy is bound, do not allow Run-Test vehicles on the road for either county engagement.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through how ballots physically get from your facility to a county tabulation center — are those your trucks, contracted carriers, or a mix?
If your driver were at-fault in a fatal accident transporting ballots, do you know what your Commercial Auto policy would actually pay out?
Both Sacramento and Maricopa require auto liability — have you ever provided the auto-line certificate to either, and did anyone push back on the limits or endorsements?
Do you have any executives driving personally-owned vehicles on company business? Has anyone evaluated that exposure on the personal auto side?

findings.requirement_type: Minimum Limits — Workers' Compensation (Sacramento + Maricopa)
findings.contract_quote: WORKERS' COMPENSATION: Statutory requirements of the State of California and Employer's Liability Insurance. ... EMPLOYER'S LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per accident for bodily injury or disease. ... Workers' compensation insurance to cover obligations imposed by Federal and State statutes ... Employer's Liability insurance of not less than $1,000,000 for each accident, $1,000,000 disease for each employee, and $1,000,000 disease policy limit.
findings.policy_quote: No Workers' Compensation policy was provided in the program submission.
findings.policy_page: N/A — no WC policy in program
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires California-statutory WC. Run-Test is AZ-domiciled — California is NOT a monopolistic state, but California-employer rules require either (a) a CA-issued WC policy, or (b) a multi-state policy with California listed in Item 3.A, NOT Item 3.C. If only 3.C 'other states' coverage is in place, California regulators can deem Run-Test uninsured for any CA work. With no WC policy in the program, this is a complete unknown.
findings.plain_english: Run-Test has 50–200 employees and is AZ-based, but the Sacramento contract requires California statutory WC the moment any employee performs work in California. We received zero workers' comp documentation. If a Run-Test employee is hurt at a Sacramento printing/sorting site and California isn't on the WC dec page in Item 3.A, the state of California can deem the company an uninsured employer — penalties, criminal exposure, and personal liability for officers under CA Labor Code §3700.5.
findings.recommendation: Obtain and audit the WC policy immediately. Confirm: (a) Arizona is in Item 3.A; (b) California is in Item 3.A (not 3.C) before any CA work begins; (c) EL limits at minimum $1M/$1M/$1M (Maricopa controlling); (d) Blanket Waiver of Subrogation endorsement (CA requires WC 04 03 06 form for CA WoS — separate premium). Also verify all 31 states Run-Test serves are properly disclosed.
discoveryQuestions: Run-Test serves clients in 31 states — how does the WC policy list them today? All in Item 3.A, or are some sitting in 'other states' coverage in 3.C?
California is the largest, most aggressive WC regulator in the country. Has anyone confirmed California is specifically on your WC policy before you sent crews to Sacramento?
If a Run-Test employee got hurt in California next month, do you know which carrier and policy would respond?
Have you ever had a WC audit reclassify your employees, and what happened to your premium?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability / Errors & Omissions (Sacramento)
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement or the beginning of Agreement performance by CONTRACTOR. B. Insurance must be maintained and evidence of insurance must be provided for at least one (1) year after completion of the Agreement. C. If coverage is cancelled or non-renewed, and not replaced with another claims made policy form with a 'Retro Date' prior to the contract effective date, the CONTRACTOR must purchase 'extended reporting' coverage for a minimum of one (1) year after completion of the Agreement.
findings.policy_quote: No Professional Liability / E&O policy was provided in the program submission.
findings.policy_page: N/A — no E&O policy in program
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires standalone E&O at $1M/$1M and explicitly bars umbrella from satisfying this minimum (§II.E). Run-Test's CORE BUSINESS is rendering professional services to election officials — ballot design/printing, mail sorting, election technology, emergency support technology. There is no E&O policy in the program submission. The D&O policy expressly excludes services rendered for fees (Endorsement #19, page 85), so it cannot fill this gap. Election services errors — wrong ballots printed, mail not delivered timely, software malfunction during certification — are textbook E&O claims. Without coverage, every county client could file a multi-million-dollar negligence suit and Run-Test pays personally.
findings.plain_english: Run-Test sells professional services to election officials. Ballot misprints, missed mail-sort deadlines, election-night technology failures are EXACTLY the type of claim E&O is designed for. The Sacramento contract demands $1M of E&O — not satisfied by any other line, not by umbrella. We received NO E&O policy. If a county sues Run-Test for a botched ballot run, there is no insurance to defend or pay. A single statewide ballot recall could be a business-ending event.
findings.recommendation: Bind a Technology / Media / Miscellaneous E&O policy immediately, claims-made, with: (a) a definition of Professional Services that explicitly includes ballot design, printing, mail sorting, election processing, election software, and emergency support technology; (b) Retro date on or before each county contract's effective date; (c) at least $1M/$1M to satisfy Sacramento, ideally $5M+ given operational scale (90M voters); (d) duty-to-defend; (e) coverage for subcontractors' work; (f) ERP options of 1, 2, 3, and 6 years. Consider stacking with a dedicated Tech E&O / Cyber combined form given the SaaS exposure.
discoveryQuestions: Run-Test's whole business is professional services to election officials — if you misprint a million ballots and a county sues, what insurance pays for that?
Has anyone shown you the definition of 'professional services' on your E&O — does it actually mention ballots, election mail, or election technology by name?
Sacramento explicitly says umbrella can't satisfy the E&O requirement. Do you know if the underlying E&O hits $1M cleanly, before umbrella?
If you cancel or switch E&O carriers next year, do you know what 'tail coverage' or 'ERP' is — and have you priced what one to three years of tail would cost on a claims-made policy?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber, Network Security & Privacy Liability (Maricopa)
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for all directors, officers, agents and employees of the Contractor, losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy ... crisis management, identity theft response costs, breach notification costs, credit remediation, and credit monitoring, defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses (data asset protection), network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: No standalone Cyber Liability policy was provided. The Crime form (PP 00 H600 00 0616) provides limited coverages: Computer Funds Transfer Fraud $2M, Deception Fraud / Social Engineering $15K, Identity Recovery $25K. Crime exclusion §V(V) (Page 55) excludes 'theft, disclosure or use of trade secrets ... or other Confidential Information ... or Data, except as covered under Insuring Agreement 7.'
findings.policy_page: Crime exclusions §V(V) and §V(H), pages 52-55 of Management Liability policy
findings.gap_description: Run-Test handles voter data for over 90 million registered voters and provides election technology / SaaS services. Maricopa requires a $5M cyber tower with very broad enumerated components: regulatory FINES and penalties (not just defense), cyber extortion, BI, computer fraud, funds transfer, third-party fidelity, no arrest-and-conviction requirement. The Crime form in the Management Liability policy covers a sliver — Computer Funds Transfer Fraud ($2M), Social Engineering ($15K only), Identity Recovery ($25K limited to natural-person officers) — but expressly EXCLUDES theft/disclosure of confidential information and Data (§V(V), p.55), excludes business-interruption / loss of income (§V(H), p.52), and provides no breach-notification, no first-party data restoration, no regulatory fines coverage. Crime is NOT a substitute for Cyber. The program is missing $5M of contractually required cyber coverage.
findings.plain_english: Run-Test sits on data for 90 million voters. Maricopa requires $5M of cyber insurance with a very specific shopping list — breach notification, ransomware, regulatory fines, business interruption, computer fraud — and the program has none of it. The Crime policy's $15K social-engineering sublimit is essentially a rounding error. A single ransomware event at an election services firm during an election cycle could shut the business down — operational outage, voter-PII regulatory action under CCPA / state breach laws, AG investigations, class actions, county breach-of-contract suits. This is the most likely catastrophic loss scenario on the company's risk profile and it is currently uninsured.
findings.recommendation: Bind a standalone Cyber Liability policy at $5M (Maricopa minimum) — strongly recommend $10M+ given voter-data scale and election-cycle visibility. Required components per Maricopa's spec: first-party (BI, dependent BI, ransomware/cyber extortion, data restoration, breach response), third-party (privacy liability, network security liability, regulatory defense AND fines/penalties where insurable, media liability), social engineering / funds transfer fraud at full cyber sublimits (NOT the Crime $15K), and explicit retroactive date predating the Maricopa contract effective date. Confirm with Coalition or comparable specialty carrier given the election-services profile. Cyber will also help backfill Sacramento's E&O requirement if written on a combined Tech E&O/Cyber form.
discoveryQuestions: Run-Test has voter records for 90 million Americans — if your network goes down 10 days before a federal election due to ransomware, what's the operational and reputational cost?

Maricopa requires $5M of cyber with regulatory fines and breach notification. The Crime policy you have only covers $15,000 of social engineering — does that match the size of the threats you're actually seeing?
Has anyone modeled what a CCPA-style class action over voter PII would cost Run-Test in a state like California?
When was the last time you had a tabletop exercise for an election-night ransomware scenario, and who pays for the 24/7 incident response retainer?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella / Excess Liability (Sacramento + Maricopa)
findings.contract_quote: UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies are acceptable where the need for higher liability limits is noted in the Minimum Limits of Insurance and shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements ... If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §II.E, Page 2 of 4 / Maricopa §8.2.9, Page 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: No Umbrella / Excess Liability policy was provided in the program submission.
findings.policy_page: N/A — no Umbrella policy in program
findings.gap_description: No umbrella policy was provided. While neither contract directly mandates an umbrella as a separate line, Maricopa's $2M Auto CSL and $5M Cyber requirements typically imply program structure with primary + umbrella stacking. Without a follow-form umbrella sitting over GL, Auto, and EL, Run-Test has no excess capacity for catastrophic claims (multi-fatality auto, statewide election disruption, mass-tort election-related litigation). For a PE-backed company at $5-25M revenue with 90M-voter exposure, an umbrella is industry standard and would normally be $10M-$25M.
findings.plain_english: Run-Test has no umbrella in the program. Even if GL/Auto/WC are eventually confirmed, primary limits run out fast. Election services has tail-risk scenarios — a multi-county certified-vote dispute, a multi-fatality vehicle accident, a coordinated cyber+physical attack on election infrastructure — where damages can dwarf primary limits. Without an umbrella, every dollar above primary is paid by the company.
findings.recommendation: Bind a follow-form Umbrella of at least $10M (industry-standard for PE-backed government contractor). Confirm: (a) follow-form over GL / Auto / EL; (b) does NOT need to follow over Professional or Cyber per Sacramento §II.E (those need to stand alone); (c) drop-down for exhausted aggregates; (d) defense outside limits if available; (e) all required underlying policies listed in schedule of underlying; (f) blanket AI / WoS / P&NC follow-form. Verify carrier rating meets A-VII (Sacramento) — Maricopa's B++ is easier.
discoveryQuestions: If a Run-Test driver caused a multi-fatality accident transporting ballots, and the verdict came in at $7M, where do the dollars above your primary auto come from?
PE-backed companies your size typically carry $10M+ of umbrella — has your sponsor or board ever asked what your excess capacity looks like?
Has anyone modeled how a contested-election lawsuit naming Run-Test as a defendant could blow through primary limits?
When you negotiated the Maricopa contract, did anyone discuss whether umbrella was expected to stack on top of the $2M auto and $5M cyber, or sit on its own?

findings.requirement_type: D&O Manufacturing & Professional Services Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: (No direct contract reference — this is a D&O coverage gap relative to Run-Test's core operational risk profile.)
findings.policy_quote: EXCLUSION FOR MANUFACTURING AND PROFESSIONAL SERVICE ENDORSEMENT: ... no coverage will be available under the Directors, Officers and Entity Liability Coverage Part for Loss for any Claim based upon, arising from, or in any way related to: (1) the malfunction of any product or product failure due to deficiency, inadequacy, defect, or dangerous condition in such product or in its design or manufacture; or (2) the rendering or failure to render any services for fees (including services for customers or clients of any Insured Entity) ...
findings.gap_description: Hartford's Manufacturing & Professional Services Exclusion bars D&O Entity Liability coverage for any claim 'arising from' rendering or failure to render services for fees, OR product failure. Run-Test's ENTIRE BUSINESS is rendering services-for-fees to election officials and manufacturing election-related products (ballots, mail). The carve-backs are narrow: (i) security-holder civil proceedings without Insured-Entity solicitation, and (ii) Derivative Actions / Demands. This means Side C (Entity) coverage is functionally nullified for the most likely D&O scenarios — a county suing the entity over service failures or product defects. Hartford Private Choice Premier consistently carries this exclusion (lessons learned 2026-03-24).
findings.plain_english: The D&O policy has a clause that strips coverage for any lawsuit arising from rendering services for fees or product defects. That IS Run-Test's business — printing ballots, sorting mail, running election software for counties for money. So if a county sues the company for blowing an election, the D&O carrier (Hartford) walks away under this exclusion unless it's a securities case or a shareholder derivative case. For a privately held PE-backed entity that mostly faces operational/customer suits, that's most of the protection gone for entity coverage. Side A protection for individual directors and officers stays largely intact — but the COMPANY's balance sheet is exposed.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate this exclusion at renewal — at minimum push for: (a) carve-back for breach-of-contract / professional-services claims by counties (often available as a manuscript endorsement on PE-backed Hartford forms); (b) move Side C entity coverage to a different carrier without this exclusion (Travelers, Chubb, AIG, Beazley); or (c) buy a separate Side A-only D&O tower at $5M-$10M (Side A doesn't trigger this exclusion as broadly because it's non-indemnifiable Insured Person Loss). The current structure leaves the entity unprotected for its highest-frequency lawsuit type. Document this exclusion explicitly to the PE sponsor — it is material to deal-level diligence.
discoveryQuestions: Your D&O has an exclusion that knocks out coverage for any lawsuit 'arising out of' rendering services for fees — and rendering services for fees IS your business. Has anyone flagged that to the PE sponsor or the board?
If Sacramento County sued Runbeck the company for negligently running their ballot operation, do you know which insurance pays for the entity's defense?
Has Hartford ever offered to negotiate this manufacturing/professional-services exclusion at renewal, and what would removing it cost?
Have you considered moving your D&O to a carrier that doesn't carry this exclusion, even at higher premium?

findings.requirement_type: Crime — Voter PII / Confidential Information Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence ... invasion of privacy (regardless of the type of media involved in the loss of private information), crisis management, identity theft response costs, breach notification costs, credit remediation, and credit monitoring ...
findings.policy_quote: No coverage for theft, disclosure or use of trade secrets ... credit card numbers, bank account numbers ... or other Confidential Information ... or Data, except as covered under Insuring Agreement 7. (Crime exclusion §V(V))
findings.gap_description: The Crime form's Confidential Information / Data exclusion explicitly bars coverage for theft or disclosure of confidential information and Data. Run-Test handles voter records for 90M+ Americans. There is no Cyber policy in program to backstop this. The narrow carve-back to Crime IA 7 (Computer Systems Restoration) is sublimited to $25,000 — utterly inadequate for a multi-state breach. Cross-references finding-005 (no Cyber policy).
findings.plain_english: If a hacker steals voter PII tomorrow, the Crime policy says: that's not covered, except for $25K of computer-restoration expense. There is no Cyber policy in the program. So a major voter-data breach lands on Run-Test's balance sheet — notification costs alone for a multi-million-record breach run $1-$3 per record (so $1M-$3M+ for a 1M-record exposure), then add forensics, credit monitoring, regulatory fines, class actions.
findings.recommendation: Address by binding standalone Cyber per finding-005. Until then, document this gap explicitly to ownership and the board. Verify Crime IA 7 (Computer Systems Restoration) sublimit — at $25K it provides no meaningful coverage for the company's actual data footprint.
discoveryQuestions: How many voter records does Runbeck touch in a typical election cycle, and have you ever priced the cost of notifying that many people if there was a breach?
If a state attorney general opened a CCPA-style investigation after a voter-data leak, who would defend Runbeck and pay the fines?
Has anyone modeled a worst-case multi-state breach scenario for Runbeck — the financial impact, not just the technical response?

findings.requirement_type: Crime — Social Engineering / Deception Fraud Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance ... computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft ... (Maricopa §8.2.13, Page 6 of 41).
findings.policy_quote: Crime — Deception Fraud / Social Engineering: $15,000 limit per occurrence (Crime Coverage Part Declarations, Page 8).
findings.gap_description: The Crime form provides only $15,000 of social engineering / deception fraud coverage. Industry-standard sublimits for a $5M-$25M revenue company range from $100K-$500K. PE-backed government contractors are a high-frequency target for vendor-impersonation wire-transfer fraud. While Maricopa's primary intent is for Cyber to absorb this, a robust Crime social-engineering sublimit is also broker best-practice.
findings.plain_english: If a Run-Test employee gets a phony email from someone pretending to be a county AP department, wires $200K to a fraudster's account, the policy covers $15,000 — the rest comes out of the company. PE-backed firms are top targets for these scams; $100K-$500K is the modern sublimit standard.
findings.recommendation: At Crime renewal, push to increase Deception Fraud / Social Engineering sublimit to at least $250,000. Pair this with full Social Engineering coverage on the recommended Cyber policy (typically $1M+ on a Coalition / Beazley form).
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Partially — but no Cyber policy in program means no second-line backstop. See finding-005.
discoveryQuestions: How does Runbeck's AP team verify wire-transfer instructions when a county changes banking details — is there a callback procedure?
If a fraudster impersonating Sacramento County tricked your team into wiring $250,000, how much of that does your current Crime policy actually pay back?
Have you ever had a near-miss on a vendor-impersonation email, and what did you change after?

findings.requirement_type: D&O / EPLI / Fiduciary Prior Acts Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: (Internal D&O coverage analysis — not a direct contract requirement)
findings.policy_quote: Prior Acts Exclusion: ... no coverage will be available for any Claim based upon, arising from, or in any way related to any Wrongful Act actually or allegedly committed before 8/18/2023, or for any Interrelated Wrongful Act thereto. (Endorsement #28, PP 00 H033 00 0616)
findings.gap_description: Endorsement #28 is a hard prior-acts cutoff at 8/18/2023, applied to D&O AND EPLI AND Fiduciary. Anything that occurred before that date — old EPL claims latent in the workforce, old fiduciary breaches, old D&O wrongful acts under the prior PE owner — is uninsurable under this policy. For a PE-backed company that may have changed sponsors and structures multiple times, this is a meaningful look-back gap.
findings.plain_english: Anything that happened before August 18, 2023 — an old harassment complaint, an old benefit-plan error, an old board decision that turns into a lawsuit later — is not covered, period. Most D&O / EPLI policies for established companies have prior-acts dates that go back many years (often 'full prior acts'). A 1-year look-back window is short, especially for a PE-owned business where claims often surface at sponsor exits.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, negotiate prior acts back as far as the current PE ownership history allows — ideally 'full prior acts' for D&O and EPLI given the operational tenure (Run-Test has 50+ years of operations). At minimum push back to the date the current PE sponsor acquired the business. If full prior acts isn't available, evaluate buying a separate Side A DIC tower with broader prior-acts coverage.
discoveryQuestions: When did the current PE sponsor acquire Runbeck, and does your policy's prior-acts date match that ownership change?
Are there any pending HR matters or old employment complaints from before 2023 that could turn into formal claims?
Has anyone discussed buying a Side A DIC tower with broader prior-acts coverage, given the PE ownership and 50-year operational history?

findings.requirement_type: D&O Split Prior or Pending Date — Upper $1M Layer
findings.contract_quote: (Internal D&O coverage analysis)
findings.policy_quote: The Prior or Pending Date for the Directors, Officers, and Entity Liability Coverage Part is amended to be 04/02/2024, but only as respects the increased Limit of Liability of $1,000,000 in excess of the first $1,000,000. (Endorsement #34, PP 00 H105 00 0616)
findings.gap_description: The upper $1M layer of D&O has a Prior or Pending Date of 4/2/2024, while the first $1M follows the master 8/18/2023 date. So any litigation/proceeding pending between 8/18/23 and 4/2/24 erodes the first $1M without access to the second $1M — creating a 'donut' where the limits are functionally only $1M for a meaningful set of matters.
findings.plain_english: Run-Test bought $2M of D&O, but only the first $1M responds to anything that was already pending between August 2023 and April 2024. If a lawsuit was simmering during that window, you effectively have $1M, not $2M. Most clients don't realize they paid for a tower that can collapse to half-strength on certain matters.
findings.recommendation: At next renewal, request a single Prior or Pending Date across both layers (preferably matching first-layer date or earlier). Confirm in writing what's pending as of 8/18/23 and 4/2/24 — knowledge of any noticeable disputes during the gap window should drive negotiation strategy.
discoveryQuestions: Were there any disputes, government investigations, or threatened lawsuits pending between August 2023 and April 2024 that the board was aware of?
Has your broker explained that your $2M D&O may only function as $1M for matters that were already in motion last year?
At renewal, has anyone asked Hartford to align both layers on a single prior-pending date?

findings.requirement_type: Crime — LLC Member Acts Exclusion (Runbeck is an LLC)
findings.contract_quote: (Internal Crime coverage analysis)
findings.policy_quote: Acts Committed By Insured's Partners or Limited Liability Members ... Loss resulting from theft, deception fraud, forgery or alteration committed by partners or LLC members. (Crime form §V(B), Page 52)
findings.gap_description: Crime exclusion §V(B) bars losses caused by partners or LLC members. Runbeck Election Services is an LLC. The narrow carve-back for IA 1 (Employee Theft) and IA 2 (Forgery) requires a specific paragraph (10) calculation that limits recovery. For a PE-backed LLC where members may include sponsor-appointed managers, this is a meaningful exclusion to understand.
findings.plain_english: Because Runbeck is an LLC and the Crime policy excludes loss from acts of LLC members, theft committed by an LLC member of the company isn't fully covered. The carve-back gets you back into the Employee Theft sublimit but it's calculated narrowly. For a PE-backed LLC, this is worth pinning down.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, ask Hartford to remove §V(B) for LLC-managed entities or to provide a broader carve-back. Alternatively, negotiate explicit member-acts coverage at full Crime sublimits.
discoveryQuestions: Who are the LLC members at Runbeck today — only PE sponsor entities, or do any individuals hold member status?
If a member-level individual were involved in a theft scheme, do you understand how the crime policy would (or wouldn't) respond?

findings.requirement_type: EPLI Wage & Hour Defense Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: (Internal EPLI coverage analysis)
findings.policy_quote: Employment Practices Liability Wage And Hour Defense Sub-Limit: $100,000. ... [Wage & Hour] is excluded ... carve-back: Defense Costs only for Wage & Hour ... subject to the Sub-Limit per Item 5.
findings.policy_page: Page 5 (Decs) and Page 35, EPLI form §V (Wage & Hour exclusion)
findings.gap_description: The EPLI form excludes wage & hour, equal pay, FLSA, and similar wage claims; only $100K of DEFENSE costs (no indemnity) is given back, and the $100K erodes the EPLI aggregate. Run-Test has 50-200 employees in a manufacturing/election-services environment with hourly election-cycle workforce. A wage-and-hour collective action is one of the most common employment claims facing this type of business. Defense alone for an FLSA collective action regularly exceeds $100K before any indemnity discussion.
findings.plain_english: If hourly election-services workers file a collective action over overtime, off-the-clock work, or misclassification, the EPLI policy covers $100K of legal defense and zero settlement dollars. FLSA defense costs blow past $100K quickly. The settlement, if there is one, is on the company.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, increase Wage & Hour Defense sublimit to $250K-$500K (carrier appetite permitting). Consider a standalone Wage & Hour policy from specialty markets if FLSA exposure is meaningful (Beazley, Hudson, AIG offer dedicated W&H forms). Pair with proactive HR audit of overtime policies and exempt classifications, especially for election-cycle temp surge workforce.
discoveryQuestions: How does Runbeck handle election-cycle overtime — straight time, time-and-a-half, comp time? Has anyone audited it against FLSA recently?
If a class-action lawyer signed up 30 of your hourly workers and filed an FLSA collective, your EPLI gives you $100K of defense costs. Is that enough for what an FLSA case actually costs to defend?
Have you ever had a DOL investigation or an employee complaint about overtime classification?

findings.requirement_type: Cancellation Notice — AZ Amendatory vs. Broker Best Practice
findings.contract_quote: Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County. (Maricopa §8.2.15, Page 7)
findings.contract_page: Maricopa §8.2.15, Page 7 of 41 / Sacramento §VI.A.2 (10-day renewal evidence)
findings.policy_quote: AZ Cancellation and Nonrenewal Endorsement: Insurer may cancel only for nonpayment with 10 days written notice by certified mail. Nonrenewal: 45 days written notice by certified mail. (Endorsement #32, HR 02 H003 01 0711)
findings.gap_description: The AZ amendatory provides 10-day nonpayment notice and 45-day nonrenewal notice. Maricopa requires 30 days notice on ANY cancellation/material change, with a 2-business-day pass-through obligation on the insured. The carrier-side notice obligation is to the insured only — Maricopa is NOT named on a Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation endorsement. Sacramento §VI.A.2 places notice obligation on the contractor. Functionally compliant under contract language, but well short of the 90-day broker-target benchmark and creates pressure on Run-Test's internal compliance to relay notices within 2 business days. No Designated Entity NOC endorsement is on file.
findings.plain_english: If Hartford cancels the Management Liability policy, Maricopa expects 30 days notice. The carrier only has to give Run-Test 10 days for nonpayment. Run-Test has to forward that notice to the County within 2 business days. The system is fragile — one missed email and Run-Test breaches the contract. There's no endorsement giving Maricopa direct notice from Hartford.
findings.recommendation: Add a Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation endorsement listing Maricopa County (and Sacramento County) as designated certificate holders entitled to direct notice from the carrier. This is typically a no-cost endorsement on Hartford forms. Establish internal SOP: ANY notice from Hartford routed to a single risk-management mailbox with 2-business-day SLA to forward to county risk managers.
discoveryQuestions: If Hartford sent Runbeck a cancellation notice tomorrow, who at Runbeck would get it, and how quickly would it reach the county risk managers?
Has anyone added Maricopa or Sacramento to a Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation endorsement so the carrier notifies the counties directly?
What's your internal SOP for forwarding insurance notices, and has it been tested?

findings.requirement_type: Carrier Rating — A.M. Best A-VII (Sacramento)
findings.contract_quote: Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII.
findings.policy_quote: Twin City Fire Insurance Co. (a Hartford company) — Hartford carriers consistently hold A.M. Best A+ XV financial strength.
findings.gap_description: Twin City Fire / Hartford comfortably exceeds both Sacramento's A-VII threshold and Maricopa's B++ threshold. Verify at COI issuance the rating is current.
findings.plain_english: The Hartford-affiliate carrier behind this policy is one of the strongest balance sheets in the business. Both counties' rating thresholds are easily met.
findings.recommendation: No action — confirm carrier rating on COI annually; this is the easy part of the program. Apply same scrutiny to any future Cyber, GL, Auto, WC, E&O carriers — surplus lines / E&S placements are common in election services and need rating confirmation.

findings.requirement_type: D&O Notice Manager Limited to CEO/CFO (Notice & Knowledge)
findings.contract_quote: (General All Policies RMF #4 — Notice and Knowledge of Claims)
findings.policy_quote: Notice Manager means the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer of the Named Entity. (Endorsement #10, PP 00 H022 00 0616)
findings.gap_description: Endorsement #10 limits the Notice Manager (the persons whose knowledge triggers notice obligations) to CEO and CFO. This is industry best-practice: a low-level employee's knowledge of an incident does NOT impute to the company and trigger forfeiture of coverage for late notice.
findings.plain_english: If a junior HR employee learns about a potential claim and doesn't tell anyone for six months, the policy doesn't lose coverage — only knowledge by the CEO or CFO starts the notice clock. This is a meaningful protective endorsement.
findings.recommendation: Replicate this Notice & Knowledge structure on EVERY policy in the program (GL, Auto, Cyber, E&O once bound). Many carriers offer it for free; others require negotiation. Ensure consistency across the tower.

findings.requirement_type: PE Co-Defendants Extension — Lincoln Shields & Black Mountain
findings.contract_quote: (PE-specific D&O coverage relevant to Run-Test's ownership)
findings.policy_quote: Co-Defendant(s) Extension Endorsement — Private Equity or Venture Capital Funds: Lincoln Shields, LLC and Black Mountain Investment Company, LLC. (Endorsement #33, PP 00 H050 00 0616)
findings.gap_description: The policy explicitly extends D&O / EPLI / Fiduciary coverage to Co-Defendants Lincoln Shields and Black Mountain Investment Company when joined to a Claim by reason of their ownership/management control of Runbeck. Coverage is conditioned on (i) actual or alleged Wrongful Act of an Insured, (ii) Claim first against the Insured, (iii) Co-Defendants joined for ownership control, (iv) same counsel. This is appropriate PE-sponsor protection.
findings.plain_english: The PE owners — Lincoln Shields and Black Mountain — get coverage when they're sued alongside Runbeck purely because they own/control Runbeck. This is exactly the protection a PE-backed company should have so the sponsor and the operating company can defend together.
findings.recommendation: Continue this endorsement at renewal. If sponsor structure changes (new fund, exit, merger), update the named co-defendants immediately. Confirm the Shadow Director extension (Endorsement #9, page 73) remains in place — it complements this and brings PE board observers into Manager status.

findings.requirement_type: D&O Shadow Director Extension
findings.contract_quote: (PE-specific D&O coverage)
findings.policy_quote: Manager now includes de facto or shadow directors acting on behalf of Insured Entity with written indemnification agreement. (Endorsement #9, PP 00 H125 00 0718)
findings.gap_description: PE board observers and shadow directors who lack formal director title but exert direction over the company are brought into Manager definition for D&O purposes (subject to written indemnification agreement). Important for PE governance models where sponsors place observers/advisors on the board.
findings.plain_english: PE sponsors often have people sitting in board meetings without an official director title. This endorsement says those people get D&O coverage too, as long as the company has agreed to indemnify them in writing. Standard PE-best-practice protection.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Confirm written indemnification agreements exist for any shadow directors / board observers — without them, this extension doesn't trigger.

findings.requirement_type: Crime — Employee Theft / Computer Fraud / Funds Transfer at $2M
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance ... computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft ... (Maricopa §8.2.13)
findings.policy_quote: Employee Theft: $2,000,000; Forgery or Alteration (incl. credit cards): $2,000,000; Computer Fraud / Funds Transfer Fraud: $2,000,000; Inside Premises: $2,000,000; Outside Premises: $2,000,000.
findings.gap_description: Crime IAs sit at $2M across most insuring agreements. This is appropriate for the company size and provides meaningful Employee Theft / Computer Fraud / Funds Transfer protection — though does NOT close the $5M Maricopa cyber gap (different coverage type, see finding-005).
findings.plain_english: If an employee steals $1M, the policy pays. If a hacker fraudulently moves $1M of funds via wire fraud, the policy pays. Both at $2M each. That's solid for a company of Runbeck's size — though it's not the same as having a real Cyber policy for the broader voter-data exposure.
findings.recommendation: Maintain $2M sublimits at renewal. Increase Social Engineering sublimit (currently $15K — see finding-009). Confirm Third-Party Coverage / Client Property if Runbeck handles client funds or property in trust.

findings.requirement_type: EPLI Third-Party Liability $1M
findings.contract_quote: (EPLI scope evaluation)
findings.policy_quote: Employment Practices Liability Third Party Discrimination/Harassment Sub-Limit: $1,000,000.
findings.gap_description: Third-party EPLI sublimit at full EPLI limit ($1M aggregate) covers harassment/discrimination claims by non-employees (e.g., poll workers, county employees, election observers). Material for a company that interacts with diverse public-sector personnel.
findings.plain_english: If a county employee or poll worker sues Runbeck claiming harassment by a Runbeck employee, EPLI responds up to $1M. That's the right structure given Runbeck's heavy interaction with county workforces.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Train on third-party harassment situations especially during high-pressure election cycles where temp workforce sizes spike.

findings.requirement_type: EPLI Retaliation — Broad Definition (Whistleblower / FCA / SOX)
findings.contract_quote: (EPLI scope evaluation — relevant to PE-backed regulatory exposure)
findings.policy_quote: Amended Definition of Retaliation: workers' comp rights, FMLA, ERISA, ADA, refusing to violate law, cooperating with investigations, whistleblower claims (False Claims Act, SOX). (Endorsement #13, PP 00 H433 00 0417)
findings.gap_description: Broad Retaliation definition expressly captures False Claims Act / SOX / whistleblower scenarios. Important given Runbeck's government-contracting profile — employees raising election-integrity or qui-tam concerns could otherwise be excluded under narrower retaliation language.
findings.plain_english: If a Runbeck employee blows the whistle on a government-contract issue or election-integrity concern and gets terminated, the EPLI covers retaliation defense. For a federal-and-state government contractor, that's exactly the right protection.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Pair with strong internal whistleblower policies and intake mechanisms.

findings.requirement_type: D&O Books and Records / Section 220 Coverage $500K
findings.contract_quote: (D&O scope evaluation — relevant to PE governance)
findings.policy_quote: Books and Records Request Endorsement: $500,000 sublimit, part of (not in addition to) Investigation Costs sublimit. (Endorsement #1, PP 00 M138 00 0421)
findings.gap_description: Books-and-records demand coverage (Delaware §220 / similar) at $500K is solid for a PE-backed entity. Helpful in pre-litigation discovery / shareholder-fight scenarios.
findings.plain_english: If a sponsor or co-investor demands access to corporate books and records as a precursor to litigation, the policy covers up to $500K of legal and forensic costs to respond. Important for PE-backed governance where information disputes are common.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Confirm sublimit is sufficient given sponsor structure complexity.

findings.requirement_type: D&O / EPLI / Fiduciary Single Highest Retention Rule
findings.contract_quote: (D&O / EPLI / Fiduciary scope evaluation)
findings.policy_quote: Single Retention — Claims Covered Under Multiple Coverage Parts: When a Claim triggers multiple Coverage Parts, only the HIGHEST applicable Retention applies — no stacking. (Endorsement #29, PP 00 H109 00 0517)
findings.gap_description: When a single claim triggers multiple coverage parts (e.g., a wrongful-termination + retaliation case touching D&O and EPLI), only the highest applicable retention is paid — not stacked retentions. Insured-favorable.
findings.plain_english: If a single lawsuit hits two parts of the policy at once, you pay one retention, not two. That's the right way the policy should work.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: D&O Personal Profit Exclusion — Final Adjudication Standard
findings.contract_quote: (D&O scope evaluation)
findings.policy_quote: Personal profit exclusion now triggered only by judgment or non-appealable final adjudication. Carve-back for Securities Act §§11, 12, 15 violations. (Endorsement #14, PP 00 H363 00 0718)
findings.gap_description: Final non-appealable adjudication is the most insured-favorable conduct-exclusion trigger. Allegation alone or interim finding does NOT lock out coverage — coverage continues through appeals. Standard best-practice for PE-backed D&O.
findings.plain_english: An allegation of personal profit doesn't kill D&O coverage — only a final, non-appealable judgment does. So insureds can defend through appeals with the policy responding. This is the correct trigger.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Replicate on any future excess D&O.

findings.requirement_type: ERP — Multi-Tier Options 12/24/36 Months
findings.contract_quote: If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: ... If coverage is cancelled or non-renewed ... the CONTRACTOR must purchase 'extended reporting' coverage for a minimum of one (1) year ... (Sacramento §V) ... an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years ... (Maricopa §8.2.3)
findings.policy_quote: Multiple Extended Reporting Period Options: (1) 12 mo @ 150% premium; (2) 24 mo @ 175% premium; (3) 36 mo @ 200% premium. (Endorsement #25, PP 00 H025 00 0616). Plus Endorsement #20 — 90-day election period.
findings.gap_description: 12/24/36 ERP options at reasonable premium multiples cover both Sacramento (1 year minimum) and Maricopa (2 years minimum) ERP requirements for the claims-made portions of the program. 90-day election window is favorable. Note: contract ERP requirements primarily target Cyber and E&O — neither of which is currently in the program (see findings 4 and 5).
findings.plain_english: The Management Liability policy lets Runbeck buy a 1-, 2-, or 3-year tail at known prices if the policy ever ends. Both county contracts will be satisfied for the lines this policy covers. The bigger issue is that neither county is really worried about D&O tails — they care about Cyber and E&O tails, which aren't in the program yet.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. When binding Cyber and E&O, negotiate similar multi-tier ERP options on those policies. Document county ERP requirements in renewal-decision SOPs.

findings.requirement_type: EPLI Workplace Violence Expense Coverage
findings.contract_quote: (Internal EPLI evaluation — relevant to election-cycle environment)
findings.policy_quote: Workplace Violence Coverage Endorsement: $100,000 sublimit. Pays BI Expenses up to 90 days, Employee salary/wages up to 90 days, counseling, security guard up to 30 days, security consultant, PR firm. NO Retention. (Endorsement #31, PP 00 H426 00 0616)
findings.gap_description: Workplace Violence Expense coverage at $100K with $0 retention provides crisis response funding (counseling, security, PR) following a violent incident. NOTE: Coverage is EXPENSE only — does NOT cover third-party liability suits. Election environments have heightened violence risk. Pair with strong physical security at facilities and during election cycles.
findings.plain_english: If a violent incident happens at a Runbeck facility, the policy pays up to $100K of crisis response — counselors, extra security, PR support — with no deductible. It does NOT pay for any lawsuits that follow the incident; those go to GL or other coverage. Useful in today's election-related security environment.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Verify physical security protocols. Consider a standalone Active Shooter / Active Assailant policy for higher limits if the election-cycle threat profile warrants — those forms also cover third-party liability that this endorsement does not.

findings.requirement_type: Anti-Trust Sublimit (D&O)
findings.contract_quote: (D&O scope evaluation)
findings.policy_quote: Antitrust/Sherman/Clayton/FTC violations subject to sublimit of lesser of remaining limit or $1,000,000. (Endorsement #16, PP 00 H377 00 0120)
findings.gap_description: Antitrust matters are sublimited to lesser of remaining D&O limit or $1M. Carve-back from full exclusion is positive, but $1M is thin given the concentrated election services market and possible federal antitrust scrutiny of vendor consolidation.
findings.plain_english: If the FTC or DOJ comes knocking on antitrust grounds — and the election services industry has a small number of major vendors, which is exactly what attracts antitrust scrutiny — the D&O caps at $1M. Antitrust defense costs alone routinely exceed $5M. The carve-back beats a total exclusion, but it's tight.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, push to remove the antitrust sublimit or increase to full D&O limit. If sponsor is rolling up election-services competitors, this becomes urgent. Consider standalone Antitrust insurance if M&A activity is meaningful.
discoveryQuestions: Is the PE sponsor pursuing roll-up M&A in the election-services space, or considering acquisitions of other vendors?
Has Runbeck or its sponsor ever received an antitrust inquiry, civil investigative demand, or HSR-related issue?
If the FTC opened an antitrust investigation tomorrow, do you understand your coverage caps at $1M?

findings.requirement_type: Workplace Violence — No Third-Party Liability
findings.contract_quote: (Internal coverage analysis — relevant to election environment threat profile)
findings.policy_quote: [Workplace Violence Endorsement] explicitly excludes 'any legal costs, attorneys fees, expenses, settlements, judgments, penalties or other amounts incurred as a result of any claim, suit or other legal proceeding brought against an Insured in connection with a Workplace Violence Action.' (Endorsement #31, page 102)
findings.gap_description: Workplace Violence Endorsement is EXPENSE coverage only. Third-party suits — wrongful death by victim's family, premises-liability claim, negligent-security suit — are NOT covered here. Those would need to flow to GL (not in program — see finding-001) or Active Assailant standalone coverage.
findings.plain_english: The Workplace Violence endorsement helps with crisis response costs but does NOT pay legal claims if survivors or victims' families sue Runbeck after an incident. With no GL policy in the program, those liability suits are uninsured. In today's elevated election-environment threat landscape, this is a real gap.
findings.recommendation: Bind GL with no workplace-violence carve-out (most modern GL forms do not exclude); evaluate a standalone Active Assailant / Active Shooter policy with combined first-party expense + third-party liability for up to $5M+.
discoveryQuestions: Have you done a security review of your facilities given the elevated threat environment around election work?
If a violent incident at a Runbeck facility led to wrongful-death suits by victims' families, what insurance pays for those lawsuits?
Has anyone priced a standalone Active Assailant policy that combines first-party expense with third-party liability?

findings.requirement_type: RMF General — Unintentional Errors & Omissions Giveback
findings.contract_quote: (General All Policies RMF #2 — broker best practice, no direct contract reference)
findings.policy_quote: No Unintentional E&O endorsement is identified in the endorsement schedule. Imputation of knowledge is amended by Endorsement #4 (PP 00 H052 00 0616) for the Application only — not the same as a UE&O giveback for unreported exposures during the policy term.
findings.gap_description: The RMF benchmark expects an Unintentional Errors & Omissions giveback so that an inadvertent failure to report a location, exposure, or operation does not result in coverage denial. Endorsement #4 narrows imputation of knowledge in the Application but does NOT provide a UE&O giveback for in-policy reporting. Need to confirm with Hartford whether the underlying form provides an embedded UE&O giveback or if a separate endorsement is available.
findings.plain_english: Most well-structured policies have a 'we won't deny coverage just because you forgot to mention something' clause. The Hartford application-imputation endorsement isn't the same thing. Need to confirm whether this protection is embedded in the master form or is missing and should be added.
findings.recommendation: Submit written request to Hartford to confirm whether an Unintentional E&O giveback exists in the master form (Common Terms) or is available as an endorsement. If neither, request it at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: RMF General — Named Insured / Subsidiary Coverage
findings.contract_quote: (General All Policies RMF #3 — Named Insureds list)
findings.policy_quote: Named Insured: Runbeck Election Services, LLC. No Additional Named Insureds listed. Endorsement #11 (PP 00 H113 00 0517) extends Subsidiary definition to controlled 501(c)(3) organizations / foundations / PACs.
findings.gap_description: Only Runbeck Election Services, LLC is listed as Named Insured — no related entities (PE sponsor entities, holding companies, IP-holding LLCs, real estate LLCs) are scheduled. The form's automatic Subsidiary inclusion may pick up controlled subs, but this is form-specific (most D&O forms include >50% owned subs automatically). Need to confirm: (a) full corporate structure / org chart, (b) whether all related entities are intended to be insured, (c) whether sponsor-side entities are properly separated by the Co-Defendants Endorsement (#33) which we know names Lincoln Shields and Black Mountain.
findings.plain_english: The policy only names Runbeck Election Services LLC. We need a current org chart to confirm whether there are other entities — IP-holding LLCs, real-estate LLCs, holding companies — that should be on the policy or already are via the automatic Subsidiary definition. Common gap in PE-owned structures.
findings.recommendation: Obtain current Runbeck org chart from CFO. Verify all operating entities, subsidiaries, holding companies, and IP-holders are either (a) automatically picked up under D&O Subsidiary definition, or (b) added as Additional Named Insureds. Replicate on every other policy in the program once bound.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Civil Code §2782 Carve-Out (AI Active-Negligence Limit)
findings.contract_quote: Coverage shall not extend to any indemnity coverage for the active negligence of the additional insured in any case where an agreement to indemnify the additional insured would be invalid under Subdivision (b) of Section 2782 of the Civil Code.
findings.policy_quote: N/A — no GL policy in program; AI endorsement compliance cannot be evaluated.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento's California Civil Code §2782(b) carve-out is a contract-level public-policy acknowledgment — it does NOT require a special endorsement. However, when a GL is bound, the AI endorsement should not contradict this carve-out. Cannot evaluate without a GL policy in the program (see finding-001).
findings.plain_english: California public policy says you can't be required to insure a county for the county's own active negligence. When the GL is finally bound, the AI endorsement just needs to not directly conflict with that — most ISO forms don't.
findings.recommendation: Once GL is bound, confirm AI endorsement (CG 20 10 + CG 20 37 or equivalent) does not contradict §2782(b). No standalone endorsement required.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Deductible/SIR Bond or Letter of Credit Risk
findings.contract_quote: Such deductible and/or self-insured retentions shall not be applicable with respect to the coverage provided to County under such policies. Contractor shall be solely responsible for the deductible and/or self-insured retention and County, at its option, may require Contractor to secure payment of such deductibles or self-insured retentions by a surety bond or an irrevocable and unconditional letter of credit.
findings.policy_quote: Management Liability retentions: D&O $10K / EPLI $10K / Fiduciary $0 / Crime IA-1 $25K. (Master Decs Page 2-8). Cannot evaluate other lines (GL/Auto/WC/Cyber/E&O) — not in program.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa reserves the right to require collateral (bond or LOC) backing for deductibles and SIRs. Cyber programs typically have $25K-$100K SIRs, E&O $25K-$100K, GL $5K-$25K. Cumulative SIRs across a future complete program could trigger a meaningful bond/LOC demand from Maricopa, especially given high contract sensitivity (election services).
findings.plain_english: Maricopa can ask Runbeck to post a bond or letter of credit equal to all the deductibles in the program. Once Cyber, E&O, GL, Auto, and WC are added, those retentions can stack to $100K+. A bond or LOC ties up working capital. This isn't a coverage issue but a real cash-flow risk.
findings.recommendation: Build the program with retentions in mind. Once GL/Auto/WC/Cyber/E&O are bound, calculate aggregate SIR exposure and discuss with Maricopa Risk Manager BEFORE they invoke the bond/LOC clause. Consider deductible buy-down endorsements where premium-efficient.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Indemnity Not Limited by Insurance Limits
findings.contract_quote: The amount and type of insurance coverage requirements set forth herein will in no way be construed as limiting the scope of the indemnity in this section.
findings.policy_quote: N/A — no policy directly addresses balance-sheet exposure above limits.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's indemnification flows through Arizona comparative-negligence rules but is NOT capped at insurance limits. Combined with the missing GL/Cyber/E&O/Umbrella policies, Run-Test's net exposure on a Maricopa claim above limits is the entire balance sheet. Even when policies are bound, the company should evaluate worst-case exposure scenarios (multi-fatality, mass-tort, statewide election disruption) where damages could exceed any reasonable tower.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's indemnification clause says: whatever insurance you buy, the indemnification obligation isn't limited by it. So if a $25M claim hits and you have $10M of insurance, Run-Test owes the remaining $15M. With several required policies missing today, the gap is much wider. This drives the case for an aggressive umbrella tower and broad primaries.
findings.recommendation: Once primaries are bound, structure umbrella/excess to at least 2x-3x Maricopa's contract minimums. Discuss with PE sponsor whether captive / SIR strategy makes sense long-term given annual exposure profile.
discoveryQuestions: Has the PE sponsor ever stress-tested what a $20M claim against Runbeck would do to the balance sheet, and how much of it would land on equity?
Maricopa's indemnification isn't capped at your insurance — has anyone modeled the gap between policy limits and worst-case exposure?
Have you considered a captive structure for the higher-frequency / lower-severity exposures to free up capacity in the commercial program?

findings.requirement_type: Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation — Maricopa & Sacramento
findings.contract_quote: Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County. ... Contractor must provide to Maricopa County, within two business days of receipt, if they receive notice of a policy that has been or will be suspended, canceled, materially changed for any reason, has expired, or will be expiring.
findings.policy_quote: designated_entity_noc_endorsements: [] (none on file)
findings.gap_description: No Designated Entity NOC endorsement is on file. Compliance is being achieved through the contractor's manual notice obligation under Maricopa §8.2.15. Best practice is direct carrier-to-county notice via Designated Entity NOC endorsement (Hartford's HSB-equivalent or CG 20 12). Adds no premium, removes operational risk of missing the 2-business-day pass-through window.
findings.plain_english: Hartford should notify Maricopa and Sacramento DIRECTLY when something changes — not rely on Runbeck to forward the email within 2 business days. One missed email is a contract breach. Adding a Designated Entity NOC endorsement is a no-cost fix.
findings.recommendation: Endorse Maricopa County and Sacramento County (and any other county with similar requirements) onto a Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation form. Replicate on every other policy in the program (GL, Auto, WC, Cyber, E&O once bound).
discoveryQuestions: Today, if Hartford sent a cancellation notice, does anyone at Maricopa or Sacramento receive a copy directly, or only through Runbeck?
What's your internal SOP if a cancellation notice arrives during a county election cycle?
Has anyone added the counties to a Designated Entity NOC endorsement on each policy in the program?

findings.requirement_type: Property / Course of Construction (Conditional)
findings.contract_quote: Any Course of Construction (COC) policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall contain the following provisions: 1. The COUNTY shall be named as loss payee. 2. The Insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: N/A — COC requirement is conditional. Election services manufacturer does not perform construction work.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento's COC requirement is conditional — it only triggers if Run-Test maintains a Course of Construction / Builders Risk policy. Run-Test as an election services manufacturer is not engaged in construction. N/A pending confirmation that Run-Test does not perform any construction work for Sacramento County.
findings.plain_english: This requirement only applies if Runbeck does construction work. As an election-services manufacturer, you don't — so this section doesn't bite. Worth confirming there are no facility build-outs or improvements being done for the County under the contract.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with Sacramento that no construction-type scope is included. If any tenant improvements, equipment installation, or facility build-outs are involved, evaluate Builders Risk requirement.

findings.requirement_type: Inland Marine Waiver of Subrogation (Conditional)
findings.contract_quote: Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: N/A — no Inland Marine policy provided in the program submission. Election services typically carries IM for mobile equipment, ballots in transit, and computer/election technology equipment.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento's IM Waiver requirement is conditional — only triggers if Run-Test carries Inland Marine. For an election services company moving ballots and election technology between facilities and county sites, IM coverage on transit/property-of-others/EDP equipment is industry standard. We received no IM policy. Need to confirm whether IM exists outside this submission.
findings.plain_english: Runbeck moves ballots, mail, and election equipment around the country. That's textbook Inland Marine. We don't have any IM documentation. If IM exists, it needs a Waiver of Subrogation in favor of Sacramento. If it doesn't, that's a meaningful uninsured property exposure on equipment in transit.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Inland Marine status. If exists, confirm Waiver of Subrogation endorsement — preferably blanket. If not, evaluate need given Runbeck's equipment in transit, voter-mail in process, and high-value election technology assets. Common limit structures: $250K-$5M depending on TIV.
discoveryQuestions: How is ballots-in-transit and equipment-in-transit insured today — IM policy, on the auto, or uninsured?
What's the total value of election technology equipment, computers, and printing presses sitting at Runbeck and at county sites at any given time?
If a truck full of printed ballots was destroyed in transit, what insurance would replace them, and would Runbeck miss the election deadline?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Per-Project Aggregate (CG 25 03)
findings.contract_quote: Contractors and Contractors engaged in other projects of construction shall have their general liability Aggregate Limit of Insurance endorsed to apply separately to each job site or project, as provided for by Insurance Services Office form CG-2503 Amendment-Aggregate Limits of Insurance (Per Project).
findings.policy_quote: N/A — only triggered by construction projects.
findings.gap_description: Per-project aggregate requirement is construction-specific. Run-Test as election services manufacturer is not implicated unless physical construction work is involved.
findings.plain_english: This only applies if you're doing construction. You're not. So this requirement doesn't trigger.
findings.recommendation: Confirm scope. If GL is eventually bound and any construction-adjacent work emerges (facility improvements, equipment installation), revisit.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Claims-Made Retro Date — Cyber
findings.contract_quote: In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed.
findings.policy_quote: N/A — no Cyber policy in program. Cannot verify retro date predating 11/01/2021 contract effective date.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's claims-made requirement (retro date predating contract effective date AND 2-year ERP) is a known specification for Cyber. Without a Cyber policy in the program, this can't be evaluated. Once Cyber is bound, retro date MUST predate the Maricopa contract effective date (per the contract: 11/01/2021). If retro is set to 'inception' on a new policy, it WILL be in breach.
findings.plain_english: When Cyber is bound, the retro date has to go back to before November 2021 (Maricopa's contract effective date). Cyber carriers often default to the policy inception date. That would breach Maricopa from day one. This is the kind of detail that gets missed at binding and bites later.
findings.recommendation: When binding Cyber, request a retro date of 11/01/2021 OR 'full prior acts' (preferred). Document this in writing to the carrier. Same for E&O. If continuous coverage is later interrupted, exercise ERP for 2 years per Maricopa. Same scrutiny applies to E&O for Sacramento contract effective date.
discoveryQuestions: When you bind Cyber and E&O, the retro date controls whether old incidents are covered. Has anyone discussed setting retro back to your earliest county contract effective date?
If a voter-data breach surfaces six months from now but the underlying intrusion was three years ago, does your retro date allow coverage?
Have you ever had a claim denied because of a retro-date issue on a claims-made policy?

findings.requirement_type: RMF General — Waiver of Subrogation Cross-Program
findings.contract_quote: (General All Policies RMF #5 + Sacramento §VIII WC waiver + Maricopa §8.2.8 program-level WoS)
findings.policy_quote: Management Liability checklist: waiver_of_subrogation: false. WoS not relevant to D&O / EPLI / Fiduciary in standard structure (these aren't lines where WoS is contractually required by Maricopa or Sacramento — both contracts EXCLUDE E&O from WoS requirement). Cross-program WoS cannot be verified for GL/Auto/WC/Cyber — those policies are missing.
findings.gap_description: Both contracts require WoS on GL/Auto/WC/Cyber/Umbrella (Maricopa explicitly carves out WC waiver in §8.2.12). E&O / Professional is excluded by both. Management Liability isn't typically subject to WoS. Cannot evaluate program-wide compliance with policies missing. When primaries are bound, Blanket WoS is the standard ask.
findings.plain_english: Once the missing policies are bound, every required line should have a Blanket Waiver of Subrogation in favor of any party where required by written contract. WoS isn't typically on D&O/EPLI/Fiduciary, so the Management Liability policy isn't the issue. The issue is verifying it's on each new line at bind.
findings.recommendation: When binding GL, Auto, WC, Cyber, and Umbrella: confirm Blanket Waiver of Subrogation endorsement is in place on each. WC requires state-specific WoS form (e.g., CA WC 04 03 06 for CA work, AZ equivalent for AZ). Verify language is 'best practices' (any party where required by written contract — no narrow carve-outs).

findings.requirement_type: Subcontractor Pass-Through Insurance Requirements
findings.contract_quote: CONTRACTOR shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of all its subcontractors and additional insured endorsements as provided by CONTRACTORs subcontractor.
findings.policy_quote: N/A — subcontractor management is a contract-administration item, not a coverage item. However, Crime IA exclusion §V(B) and the D&O Manufacturing/Professional Services Exclusion both have implications if subs are involved.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento makes Run-Test responsible for subcontractor acts AND for ensuring subs provide AI endorsements to the County. Best practice: maintain a vendor insurance program with documented insurance requirements equal to or greater than what Sacramento demands. Need to confirm Run-Test has a subcontractor insurance compliance program.
findings.plain_english: When you use subcontractors on the Sacramento contract, Sacramento expects YOU to make sure those subs have proper insurance and have named the County as additional insured. If a sub creates a problem and the sub's insurance fails, Runbeck is on the hook. Need a documented vendor insurance compliance process.
findings.recommendation: Implement a vendor insurance compliance program: (a) standard insurance requirements language in every sub agreement matching county requirements; (b) sub COIs collected and tracked annually; (c) AI endorsement copies (not just COI references) collected; (d) annual audit. Common platforms: myCOI, Ebix, Riskonnect.
